sources.title: Geological map of Greenland 1:2 500 000
sources.authors: Jan C. Escher and T. Christopher R. Pulvertaft
sources.publisher: Geological Survey of Greenland (GGU); official digital copy hosted by GEUS
sources.page: Single sheet, PDF page 1; southeastern Inland Ice and glaciated margin around 65.5–68.5°N near 40°W, full graticule context and Inland Ice legend.
sources.supports: Regional ice-sheet and marginal feature-class context, distinguishing glacier, fjord and settlement names from evidence of a named river.
sources.limits: Regional geological mapping, not a river gazetteer or hydrological survey. It supports the feature-class scope conclusion, not proof of natural flow, connectivity or formal river identity. The historical ice margin is not asserted to be its current position.
sources.reuse_limit: GEUS custom terms allow internal research but restrict redistribution and new maps based on the data. The original map and local crops remain private; only own factual notes and public bibliography are intended for publication.

correspondence: The complete selected one-piece mainstem was inspected. Its northern beginning is near 68.5°N, with a short southwestward approach followed by long nearly straight southward legs and small westward offsets. A short southeastward final segment ends near 65.5°N. No separate tributary fragment is selected. These are descriptions of the generalized model, not proof of a natural channel.

The original geological sheet, its visible longitude and latitude graticule, and a newly rendered southeastern regional view place the long northern and middle route within the mapped Inland Ice. The southern continuation approaches the southeastern glaciated margin west of the Tasiilaq/Ammasalik coastal region. Nearby settlement, glacier and fjord names are orientation anchors only; none is transferred to the complete modeled line.

No readable source establishes a natural-river hydronym for this complete ice-sheet path. Its very long modeled interior legs cannot be treated as a named river merely because a downstream ice-margin area contains natural drainage. This is a completed feature-class and name-scope assessment, not a claim that every surface, subglacial or marginal watercourse is unnamed.

The original Inland Ice legend distinguishes ice-surface contours, dashed thickness isopachs, sub-ice bedrock contours and aeromagnetic lineaments south of 68°N. The retained descriptive bulletin explains these mapped classes. Such lines do not establish current surface-water or subglacial flow along the selected geometry. The historical map margin is not asserted to be its current position.

correspondence.finding: The easternmost modeled fragment runs west through the Los Lagartos–Mirador lowland setting toward Paxbán. CONRED cartography covers this full reach and depicts its surrounding inundation-prone lowlands, settlements and intermittent drainage context, but does not label the complete selected line Candelaria or Julubal. Flood-hazard shading alone is not a mapped river or proof of continuous surface flow.

The short east–west fragment is a nearly straight, border-aligned model connection in the Paxbán sector. The official map locates this sector east of the separately labeled Río Julubal. Neither a boundary line nor surrounding lowland shading establishes that the full straight model segment is a natural, continuously connected river channel. Laguna El Paisban is nearby context; the selected line is not asserted to cross the whole lake.

The primary drainage study maps the eastern Mirador-region approach as karst valleys containing seasonal swamps and intermittent streams, with springs and inferred subsurface flow distinguished from rivers. Its evidence supports treating this modeled approach as a mixed karst-drainage corridor; it does not establish one continuous surface channel or transfer Candelaria to every selected vertex.

In western northern Petén, the selected westward and northwestward course corresponds to the channel repeatedly labeled Río Candelaria on the CONRED map, then crosses into Mexico on that corridor. The selected broad southern dip is generalized and is not promoted to a surveyed thalweg. Río Julubal enters the wider setting from the north, while Xan and Chocop lie farther south; no unsupported Julubal alias or San Pedro substitution is made.

The Mexican continuation matches Candelaria northward from the international boundary, past the California–El Toro wetland setting, through the San Miguel lake surroundings and onto the westward middle course. The municipal map directly labels this river repeatedly. Río Caribe and Arroyo Negro approach from the northeast; Las Golondrinas and the Arroyo de Cuba setting are separate eastern approaches. Adjacent lagoons are not all treated as model crossings.

The downstream selected fragment turns north on the separately labeled Candelaria course across Carmen, east of Chumpán and south of the Mamantel approach. Its end lies in the Laguna Panlao–eastern Laguna de Términos receiving setting. This supports a coastal-lagoon terminus, not an assertion that the selected line reaches the open Gulf shoreline or names the entire lagoon interior.

The selected southern piece follows a Bakhuis-side approach northward, bends west and then northeast. Holthuis Map 1 depicts the corresponding upper Nickerie corridor west of the Bakhuis Range, with Van Eeden Falls on its southern limb. The associated expedition account identifies the river above the falls as Nickerie. The first small modeled feeder and its exact source point are not separately named or fixed by this generalized map.

The long northeastward upper limb enters the northward trunk at the setting where the historical map separately draws and labels Fallawatra River from the south. The selected route arrives from the southwest; it does not trace the Fallawatra branch. The short model stage-transition piece does not by itself establish a natural confluence or hydronym boundary.

The selected trunk continues north and through pronounced middle bends rather than turning east along the separately shown Wajombo connection toward Coppename. Both institutional national maps identify this connected western corridor as Nickerie and show Corantijn farther west.

The ministry map reproduces the selected lower meander pattern and the turn northwest toward the Wageningen, Henar bridge, Steiger Ingas and Pier Ramdien settings. A separate sinuous western tributary joins the lower corridor on the map, but the selected group contains no tributary fragments and does not follow that branch southward. Its name is not assigned from the preliminary Maratakka lead or from proximity alone.

The selected terminal is in the lower Nickerie coastal/estuarine approach near Nieuw-Nickerie. The historical map and ministry report distinguish this river from Corantijn and from Nanni Creek or swamp waters. The selection is not extended into a complete Corantijn estuary or an open-ocean reach; no surveyed mouth, tidal-limit or shoreline vertex is asserted.

The northern modeled beginning runs into East Fork Thirsty Canyon and then Thirsty Canyon, joining the Amargosa River corridor near the Oasis Valley springs. West Fork Thirsty Canyon is a separate fork; Rocket Wash enters from the east. Canyon labels establish geographic correspondence without proving that the complete upper modeled line bears the Amargosa River name.

The main selected route follows repeated Amargosa River labels through Oasis Valley and Beatty, then southeast across the Amargosa Desert. Beatty Wash, Fortymile Wash and Topopah Wash are separately shown approaching from the east. The selection does not follow those tributaries as its long upstream route.

The middle and southern sections correspond to the Amargosa River through the Death Valley Junction, Shoshone, Tecopa and canyon settings. The modeled line bends west near Dumont Dunes and returns northwest past the Saratoga Spring and Confidence Hills surroundings into southern Death Valley. Federal map labels and BLM's canyon description support this distinctive route.

In Badwater Basin the selected line diverges from the mapped Amargosa channel, crosses a substantial playa interior, and continues into the separately labeled central Death Valley Salt Creek corridor. The detailed map does not show one continuously named Amargosa channel along that entire modeled connection. No through-river, exact natural terminus, or flow direction through the modeled playa extension is inferred.

The NPS water-resources account distinguishes Salt Creek and the Amargosa River and describes perennial Amargosa flow as limited to short, seasonally varying stretches. The mapped network therefore cannot be treated as evidence of continuous surface flow. BLM's year-round-flow description concerns the river's spring-supported canyon context and does not resolve the modeled playa naming problem.

scope_limit: MAIN_RIV groups and model mainstem roles do not establish a uniform name for every included reach, tributary or lake passage. Source observations support only the stated representative identity or hold.
publication_boundary: Own factual observations, attribution and official public URLs only; source originals, images, complete coordinates and private evidence remain omitted.
